turns.prompt_text: How much better is using ethernet than Wi-Fi nowadays?
turns.response_html:
Despite major leaps in wireless technology, Ethernet remains the undisputed heavyweight champion for consistency. While modern standards like Wi-Fi 7 and Wi-Fi 6E have closed the raw speed gap, they still can't compete with the physical reliability of a copper cable.

Here is how the comparison breaks down across the factors that actually affect your daily usage:

1. Latency and "Jitter"

This is the biggest differentiator. Ethernet is Full Duplex, meaning it can send and receive data simultaneously. Wi-Fi is Half Duplex (like a walkie-talkie); devices must take turns talking to the router.

  • Ethernet: Provides near-zero local latency. If you are gaming or on a professional video call, your "ping" will be rock-solid.
  • Wi-Fi: Even with a great signal, you’ll experience "jitter" (random spikes in latency) caused by interference from walls, microwaves, or even your neighbor’s router.

2. Reliability vs. Raw Speed

Ethernet standards like Cat6a or Cat8 can technically handle up to $10\text{ Gbps}$ or even $40\text{ Gbps}$, far exceeding most home internet plans.

  • Consistency: On Ethernet, if you pay for $1\text{ Gbps}$, you usually get $940\text{ Mbps}$ (after overhead) 100% of the time.
  • The Wi-Fi "Tax": Wi-Fi speeds advertised on the box (e.g., $9.6\text{ Gbps}$ for Wi-Fi 6) are theoretical maximums in a lab. In a real home, you often lose 30-50% of that speed the moment you move one room away or connect multiple devices.

3. Congestion Management

Think of Wi-Fi like a single-lane road where every device in your house (and your neighbor's house) is trying to drive.

  • Ethernet: Every plugged-in device has its own private "express lane" to the router.
  • Wi-Fi: As you add smart bulbs, phones, and tablets, the "airtime" gets crowded. Hardwiring stationary devices (like a desktop or Apple TV) actually makes your Wi-Fi better for your phone because it clears up the airwaves.

When should you bother with a cable?

You don't need to wire your whole house, but Ethernet is still "significantly better" for these specific use cases:

TaskEthernet ImpactWhy?
Competitive GamingCriticalPrevents "lag spikes" and packet loss during intense moments.
Video ConferencingHighStops the "Your connection is unstable" message and audio roboticizing.
4K StreamingMediumEliminates buffering and ensures the highest bitrate (HDR/Dolby Vision).
Large File BackupsHighSustained high speeds for gigabytes of data without dropping.

The Bottom Line: Wi-Fi is for convenience; Ethernet is for performance. If a device has a screen and doesn't move (like your workstation or a console), plugging it in is still the single best upgrade you can give your home network.
